title: Brains are not hardwired: ectopic tail eyes in tadpoles still support vision

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Brains are not hardwired: ectopic tail eyes in tadpoles still support vision

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but can ascertain the body's structure and adjust their programs; tadpoles made to develop eyes on their tails, connected to the spinal cord rather than the brain, can still see quite well.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2019, The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition › Discussion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Tadpoles engineered to develop with eyes on their tails instead of in their usual spot can see quite well, despite the fact that the eyes connect to the spinal cord, not the brain (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017). Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but are able to ascertain the structure of the body and adjust their functional programs accordingly

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition”, Frontiers in psychology (2019), doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02688; section “Discussion”. Scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes; developing nervous systems generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2019-boundary-24: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The ectopic-eye visual-performance result has clear controls and a measurable decision criterion. Public evidence may resolve that example, but raw data access is uncertain and the general claim about non-hardwired brain programs is only indirectly supported.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Analyse trial-level visual discrimination behavior and neural connectivity in tadpoles with tail-positioned eyes, comparing performance with eyeless and normally eyed controls and testing whether spinally connected ectopic eyes support above-chance vision.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trial-level behavioral and connectivity data may not be deposited.

The broad conclusion that brains ascertain body structure exceeds the ectopic-eye result.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.28
data existence: 0.38
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Visual performance with a known, abnormal projection is a sharp test of hardwiring, and the Xenopus experiments were published with behavioral results. Those results can be read as measurements and cannot be recomputed from open trial files. Xenbase locates the phenotype literature and does not hold the learning curves. The tadpole result is partly assessable from the publications; the general claim about brains exceeds that sample.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In tadpoles whose only eyes are on the tail and innervated by the spinal cord, score visual learning against blinded and orthotopic-eye controls, with innervation checked by tracing. Sight without a direct brain projection would support functional adjustment; chance performance, or a hidden projection to the brain, would refute the empirical claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trial logs and axon traces are in the papers, not a repository.

The leap from these tadpoles to brains in general is wider than the data.

Extra-ocular light sensitivity has to be excluded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.35
data existence: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.86
